records.our_prose: Asian pears flower in early spring, about the same time as other pears and a bit before apples, so a late frost can catch the open blossoms. Different varieties bloom a few days apart over about two weeks, and two trees can only pollinate each other if they bloom at the same time. One tip: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom very early and pollinate each other, but often finish before the Japanese kinds open, so match them up carefully.

records.our_prose: A long-lived deciduous fruit tree (Pyrus pyrifolia) grown for round, crisp, apple-shaped fruit, also called the apple pear, sand pear, or nashi. Asian pear is a cross-pollination crop: nearly all cultivars are self-unfruitful, so you plant two different, bloom-overlapping varieties and rely on bees to move pollen between them (a couple, like Shinseiki and 20th Century, are partially self-fruitful but still crop far better with a pollinizer). The signature difference from the European pear is at harvest: Asian pears RIPEN ON THE TREE and are eaten crisp and juicy like an apple. You pick them tree-ripe and sweet, not firm-and-green to finish indoors, and a fruit picked too early stays hard and bland. The trees set very heavily and must be thinned hard for decent fruit size. Fire blight is the major disease, worst in warm, humid regions, so cultivar and rootstock choice matter. Chill requirement is moderate and variety-set (roughly 250 to 600 hours), and rootstock choice sets mature size and how soon the tree bears.

records.our_prose: This is the most important thing about growing Asian pears: one tree alone makes only a small, unreliable crop. The flowers need pollen from a DIFFERENT Asian pear variety, carried by bees, so plant two different kinds within about 50 feet that bloom at the same time. A couple of varieties (Shinseiki, 20th Century) can set a small crop on their own, but they do much better with a partner. Two tips: the Chinese kinds (Ya Li, Tsu Li) bloom too early to pollinate the Japanese kinds, so pair them together; and a Bartlett (European) pear can pollinate Asian pears if it blooms at the same time. Once they do set fruit, expect a lot of it, so be ready to thin heavily.

records.our_prose: If your tree comes bare-root (bare roots, no pot), plant it in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless and dormant, as soon as you can dig the soil. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough that the roots spread out without folding. The key thing: find the graft union (the bumpy spot low on the trunk where the top variety was joined to the roots) and keep it about 2 to 3 in above the soil, never bury it. Fill the hole with the same soil you dug out, water well, and tie small trees to a stake. A potted tree is planted the same way and can go in anytime through spring.

records.source_context: Mainly, you want to prune a tree to have well-spaced branches and a balanced appearance, while eliminating problem branches (those that are broken, diseased or dead). Fruit trees should be pruned every year in late winter or early spring, after the coldest weather is past and before growth begins. Prune minimally, especially with young trees, as excessive pruning will delay or reduce fruiting and create too much leafy growth.

records.our_prose: Plant a bare-root tree while fully dormant, late winter to early spring, as soon as the ground is workable. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two before planting, dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending, and set the tree so the graft union (the swollen knob where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 in above the final soil line, burying it lets the variety root over and defeats the rootstock. Backfill with native soil, water in to settle, and stake dwarf and size-controlled stocks. A potted tree follows the same depth rule but can go in through spring.
